title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
description: Brute force to optimized: linear scan versus binary search on the local slope direction to find the mountain peak in O(log n).

content.title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array

blocks.text: Problem Summary: An array arr is a "mountain array" if it strictly increases up to some peak index, then strictly decreases afterward. Given such an array, return the index of the peak element.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A sorted-then-reversed-sorted (\"mountain\") shape","Binary search on the local slope direction rather than the value itself"],["\"Find the peak/turning point\" in a unimodal array","Compare arr[mid] to arr[mid+1] to decide which half still contains the peak"]]}

blocks.text: The array rises strictly to a single peak, then falls strictly. At any index mid (except the very last), comparing arr[mid] to arr[mid+1] reveals which side of the peak mid is on: if arr[mid] is smaller, the array is still climbing and the peak lies to the right; otherwise, the peak is at mid or to its left.

blocks.title: Analogy: Hiking Up and Down a Single Mountain
blocks.text: Picture hiking a trail that goes up to one summit and then down the other side, with no smaller bumps along the way. Standing at any point and looking at the very next step tells you immediately whether you are still climbing (summit ahead) or already past it (summit behind or right here).

blocks.caption: Comparing arr[mid] to arr[mid+1] reveals which half still contains the peak

blocks.text: Result: index 1 (value 1), the single peak of this mountain array.

Before scanning linearly, notice the "strictly increasing then strictly decreasing" shape means the slope direction at any midpoint is a clean binary signal, which is exactly what makes binary search on the slope (not the value) applicable here.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The array has exactly one peak, and everything to its left is strictly increasing, everything to its right is strictly decreasing.

Observation 2: At any index mid, checking whether arr[mid] < arr[mid+1] tells you unambiguously whether mid is still on the increasing side (peak is strictly to the right) or already on the decreasing side or at the peak itself (peak is at mid or to the left).

Observation 3: This lets a binary search narrow the search range by half at each step, converging on the peak index in O(log n) instead of scanning linearly.

Observation 4: The search invariant "the peak is always within [lo, hi]" is maintained by setting lo = mid+1 when still climbing, and hi = mid when already descending (or at the peak), continuing until lo equals hi.
This leads to a binary search comparing arr[mid] and arr[mid+1] at each step, narrowing the range toward the peak in O(log n) time.
Scan the array from left to right, stopping at the first index where the next element is no longer larger, which is the peak.

items: While the next element is strictly larger than the current one, move forward.
Stop and return the current index once the array stops increasing.

codes.python:
def peak_index_in_mountain_array_brute(arr):
    i = 0
    while i + 1 < len(arr) and arr[i] < arr[i + 1]:      # scan while still climbing
        i += 1
    return i

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A simple linear scan directly follows the "climb until you cannot climb anymore" definition of the peak.
It is correct, but examines up to n elements even though the mountain shape allows a much faster search.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), scanning until the peak is found.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: the strictly-increasing-then-strictly-decreasing shape allows binary search on the slope direction, finding the peak in O(log n) instead of O(n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why linear scanning is unnecessary: at any midpoint, a single comparison (arr[mid] vs arr[mid+1]) definitively tells you which half of the array still contains the peak, discarding the other half entirely.

How the search narrows: if arr[mid] < arr[mid+1], the peak must be at some index greater than mid (still climbing), so set lo = mid+1; otherwise, the peak is at mid or to its left, so set hi = mid.

Why this converges correctly: the invariant "the peak lies within [lo, hi]" is preserved at every step, and the range strictly shrinks, so when lo equals hi, that shared index is the peak.

The core idea: binary search using the LOCAL SLOPE at each midpoint as the deciding signal, rather than comparing against a target value.
Binary search with lo=0, hi=n-1. At each step, compare arr[mid] to arr[mid+1]; move lo to mid+1 if still climbing, otherwise move hi to mid. Stop when lo equals hi.

blocks.caption: Binary search on the slope direction halves the range every step

blocks.text: Because the array strictly increases then strictly decreases with exactly one peak, the comparison arr[mid] < arr[mid+1] is a perfectly reliable signal for which half contains the peak: true means the peak is strictly ahead, false means it is at or before mid. This halves the search space every iteration, converging on the exact peak index in O(log n) steps.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), halving the search range each step.
Space: O(1).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find the turning point in a strictly increasing-then-decreasing array", think: binary search on the slope direction at each midpoint.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear scan runs in O(n) time; the binary search on slope direction runs in O(log n) time, both using O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the local slope direction, rather than on a target value.
Core Idea: compare arr[mid] to arr[mid+1]; move right if still climbing, move to mid if already descending; converge to the peak.
Time: O(n) for the linear scan, O(log n) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: binary search works on any monotonic-signal midpoint check, not just direct value comparisons.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible introduction to "binary search on a condition" beyond classic value search.
One line memory trick: still climbing means go right; already descending means go left (inclusive of mid).
